2. 
The Future of Atlas Roofing. Chief Justice Roberts does “not reach 
the suggestion made by Jarkesy and Patriot28 that Tull and Graufirbarbciera 
effectively overruled Atlas Roofing'' 122 S. Ct. at 2137. In a footnote, however, 
Chief Justice Roberts states that 'Atlas Roofing represents a departure from 
our legal traditions” and offers a collection of citations to scholarship tha± 
either ignores or criticizes that precedent. Id. at 2138 n.4. The note ends with 
a disclaimer: “We express no opinion on these various criticisms.” Id. In 
response. Justice Sotomayor criticizes the majority for “leav[ing] open the 
possibihty that Granfinanciera might have overruled Atlas Roofing and 
explains why “[t]hat suggestion strains credulity.” Id. at 2168 n.8. Chief Justice 
Roberts responds to the dissent’s criticism in yet another footnote. See id. at 
2137 n.3. This below-the-line dialogue may suggest (or provoke) further 
htigation challenging Atlas Roofing.
3. 
Effects of Jarkesy on the SEC and Beyond. While Jarkesy was 
pending, the SEC voluntarily ceased using the Dodd-Frank Acts option of 
pursuing civil penalties in-house before SEC ALJs. As the Supreme Court 
notes, that option was new in 2010. This fact and the SEC’s action may suggest 
that the decision will have minimal effect on the SEC. But as Justice 
Sotomayor notes, many other agencies have statutory authority that is called 
into question by Jarkesy. EPA, which has broad authority to enforce 
environmental regulations through the administrative adjudication of 
monetary penalties may be particularly hard hit.
4. 
A Consent-Based Solution'? Regulated parties often prefer 
fl d m 1 n 1 str fl ti vo adjudication to proceedings in a federal district court. Consider 
the perspective of a large company accused by the SEC of defrauding investors: 
it may prefer a low-profile proceeding before an SEC ALJ to a higher-profile 
prosecution before a jury in federal court. Appealing to a robust version of the 
consent theory we saw in Schor^ Professors Chris Walker and David Zaring 
have argued that the solution to the problems created by Jarkesy is to offer 
regulated parties a right to remove an action from administrative adjudication 
to federal district court. See Christopher J. Walker & David Zaring, The Right 
to Remove in Agency Adjudication, 85 OHIO ST. L.J. 1 (2024). Professors Walker 
and Zaring argue that an agency could provide such a right by adopting a 
procedural rule or Congress could provide it by statute. This would neutralize
